description: We are a group of Year 10 students interested in problem-solving and engineering. We are passionate about space exploration and learning new skills.
summary: Welcome to Mars Maps! This is an interface we built to help astronauts navigate Martian terrain. Mars is a dangerous place, harbouring deadly hazards such as radiation, lethal terrain, and extreme weather. Our software’s preloaded routes improve astronaut safety by avoiding these hazards, preventing injuries and death that would otherwise be present. We acquired this data by compiling past weather patterns to predict future weather. The rigorous data we gathered comes from the Perseverance rover, which has been exploring the western face of Jezero Crater since 2021. Our predetermined routes lead to four pivotal landmarks: Three Forks at the foot of the delta, the ramp at Hawksbill Gap, the rim of Belva Crater on the delta top, and the isolated butte at Kodiak.
details:
What does it do?

Mars Maps is an interface that helps astronauts plan and walk routes across Jezero Crater, and evaluates dangers and risks before the trip allowing astronauts to make the best decision before and also during the mission by providing real time updates of incoming dangers.

The astronaut will be able to select a start point and an endpoint by clicking on the map, or pick one of the four science destinations: Three Forks, Hawksbill Gap, the rim of Belva Crater and the Kodiak butte. There will be three choices of routes, fastest, safest or the route with most science for either a return trip or one way. The risk of the journey will be shown as a number between 1-100, 1 being the lowest risk and 100 being certain death. A weather forecast for the chosen departure time in LTST will also affect the risk of the mission. The user interface is adapted to devices with limited screen space, allowing it to run on mobile devices. 

How does it work?

Four layers of data sit under the map. Surface imagery shows the terrain ahead of the Astronaut. An elevation layer to show the shape of the terrain. A slope layer marks out the steep gradients and a ground type layer to show the different surfaces the astronaut will be walking on. Radiation exposure is calculated before the trip. Weather patterns are also forecasted before starting navigation as well as warnings when sudden changes in weather conditions are detected.

Routes are found with the A* search algorithm that minimises the walking time rather than distance. Time estimates are calculated with walking speed at 2.7km/h on flat ground. Walking speed is reduced by 18% on sand and 40% among boulders using Tobler's hiking function. The safest route additionally penalises slope and any surface that is not firm ground so it maps around the hazards. Energy is calculated from the distance and surface the astronaut walks on and the physical effort of lifting crew and suit against Mars’ gravity at 3.71m/s. Oxygen is calculated from the amount of energy the astronaut is exerting, at the rate of  one liter per 20.1 kilojoules used, giving around 77 grams an hour at 300 watts. Radiation is calculated using the 0.64 millisieverts per day that Curiosity rover measured on the surface. The calculations are adjusted according to the suit mass, working effort and tank size. Routes are replanned from the selected starting spot and every figure is recalculated. 

This software is a tool designed for astronauts to make the best decisions when navigating on Mars. It is a program that combines several calculations in order to make the best decision.  Instead of asking whether a walk feels too far, the program will analyse all factors and produce a definite result for the astronaut. It not only plans routes but also works during walks. It will guide the astronaut turn by turn and call out climbs, soft sand or boulder fields as they approach it. This  ensures the astronauts are fully aware of their surroundings and essential information reaches them at the point where it matters. 

Our Goal 

This project hopes to achieve is to show that just mapping out the area is not enough for safe human exploration. Martian terrain is filled with uncertainty and this project will help the crew eliminate some of the uncertainties such as weather and hazardous terrain. The program adjusts in real time, allowing astronauts to make better decisions rather than sticking to just a map of the area. 

We want to apply our current knowledge of Mars and compile it into a program that evaluates the pros and cons of the current situation. Walking speed comes from Apollo, radiation measurements come from Curiosity and the oxygen use comes from standard physiology.  The assumptions of the astronauts can be adjusted so the astronauts can have a better idea of what parts of the calculations they are trusting. 

The communal vision is to build something that is universal and can be applied not only to the Jezero Crater but rather create a program that can be adjusted for navigating other parts of Mars. The program generates the path from existing information, so by feeding the program a different map, it can still generate the most optimal path using existing calculations. The end goal of this project is to create a tool that astronauts can carry to assist them in decision making.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Coding Languages:

Javascript: Interactive HTML model

Python: Image preparation

Algorithm used:

A* route finding, Tobler’s hiking function, Ramer-Douglas-Peuker path simplification

AI Tools

Claude AI by Anthropic was used to code the HTML

Gemini AI by Google was used to understand Martian weather data
